Let's kick this series off with #UnfairDiscrimination (MIT AI Risk 1.1) 

An employer could be accountable for a rejection decision it never saw, made by a tool it did not build.  

MIT subdomain 1.1, unfair discrimination and misrepresentation, covers unequal treatment of individuals or groups by AI, often on the basis of race, gender or other characteristics.  

In #Mobley v. Workday, a collective action in the Northern District of California, the applicant alleges he was rejected from more than 100 roles by employers using the vendors AI screening tools. In 2024 the court allowed the claim to proceed on the theory that a vendor screening candidates on an employers behalf can be its agent. A nationwide age-discrimination collective was conditionally certified in May 2025, distribution of the class action notice to potential plaintiffs was authorised in February 2026, and the core discrimination claims are still live. Workday denies the allegations and says its tools do not make hiring decisions. Nothing is proven yet.  

For lawyers, risk and governance professionals, a few points stand out.  
Discrimination does not need a protected characteristic in the data. 
A model trained on past hiring patterns can learn proxies: graduation year, employment gaps, keywords. 
At provider level, the vendor configures the ranking logic and holds most of the evidence about how it behaves. 
At deployer level, the feature may be switched on by default, with no one looking at rejection rates by age band. 
And the applicant can be rejected in minutes, without ever being told that AI was involved, which is what makes this risk so hard to detect from the inside.  

Practical steps: 
➡️Map where automated screening and ranking already sit in your hiring chain, including features enabled by default. 
➡️ Test outcomes across protected groups before go-live and at intervals afterwards, not only the design intent of the tool. 
➡️ Put bias-testing obligations, audit rights and evidence access into vendor contracts. 
➡️ Keep human review meaningful and documented. For high-risk uses under the EU AI Act, this sits with the deployer, not the provider. 
➡️ Consider in advance, how bias-testing work is commissioned and whether privilege applies.  

Buying the tool does not transfer the accountability. How is your organisation testing what its hiring tools actually do, rather than what they are intended to do?  

Explore the risks: https://airisk.mit.edu/

Is AI really going to replace all of our jobs? The panic is growing, but history shows we have been here before.

When automated machinery first hit factory floors, people predicted the absolute end of work. Instead, it birthed entirely new industries. When Excel was introduced, manual bookkeeping disappeared, but accountants did not. The ones who mastered the tool simply evolved and thrived.

Now, the same anxiety has moved to white-collar roles, and it is equally shortsighted. AI is not replacing human thinking; it is automating repetitive manual labor.

Consider how this works in practice with something like due diligence or contract review. By connecting an AI via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), software can now scan documents and flag risks in minutes. It eliminates hours of manual digging, but it cannot make the ultimate judgment call. A human still has to decide what actually matters.

This shift is also changing how we hire. I no longer look at CV experience first. I screen for sharp judgment, creative agility, and fast problem-solving. These are the traits that consistently override a long resume. This is not job replacement; it is industrial acceleration. The future of hiring belongs to qualitative talent, and the biggest opportunities will go to those who are ready to orchestrate the tech rather than fear it.

Almost 8 years in finance starting from PwC to operating inside healthcare

Moving through audit, advisory, valuation and due diligence before managing finance myself 

The most common mistake I see in HealthTech is that founders build a growth plan and a financial plan as if they were two separate documents

In my view they are the same plan because a revenue forecast is only as credible as the commercial engine behind it

So every time I look at a HealthTech business my focus is not their growth rate. But I want to know: 

- How many customers ? 
- At what contract value ? 
- Through what pipeline ? 
- At what conversion rate ? 
- And over what timeline ? 

Recently, I reviewed a growth plan ahead of a fundraise and the company wanted more sales capacity

If we talk in commercial sense then the idea is great. 
More sales people → more pipeline → more revenue.

But business is never this simple otherwise FINANCE would have become obsolete even before AI

When I ran the diagnostic it became clear to the founder and his team that each new hire would start costing cash from month one while every sale still had to move through procurement, IT, clinical sign-off, contracting and implementation before meaningful cash arrived

That is why I always tell founders not to review hiring and revenue separately but to connect them by asking:

• How long from first conversation to first cash ? 
• What does each commercial hire cost before they pay back ? 
• What happens to CAC payback when the sales cycle stretches ? 
• What pipeline coverage is needed to justify the hiring plan ? 
• Can the company fund the growth until the growth funds itself ? 

The reason is that every new hire, market, customer segment or product is ultimately a capital allocation decision and finance job is not just to budget for the growth plan

UK data and BI hiring remains steady, with mean salaries around £50,000 (up 3.7% year on year, a 16.1% premium over the national average) and demand up 7.7% year on year. Live contract listings this period reveal a wide day-rate spread, from £250 a day for customer-success-adjacent analyst work to £600 a day for banking sector and specialist PLM/Teamcenter roles, with the majority Outside IR35.

The trend worth naming: that spread is driven by sector and platform specialism, not the generic "data analyst" title. Banking, compliance, and platform-specific roles command a clear premium over broad analyst experience.

The signal to watch: Microsoft's September 2026 Power BI update now lets AI agents autonomously create and modify semantic models, alongside new administrative controls to block that access entirely. AI governance has moved from the report layer to the data model itself, and deciding where AI should and shouldn't have write access is becoming a distinct, valuable skill.

For clients building a contracting pathway: target domain exposure deliberately rather than broad tool fluency alone, and start building fluency in AI governance now, before it becomes a baseline expectation. Regionally, Scotland (Glasgow, Edinburgh) continues to show genuine contract opportunity beyond London and the South East.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance & Algorithmic Bias and its legality under nigeria employmemt laws.
‐‐--------------------------------------------------------------
As of 2026, Nigeria lacks a comprehensive AI Act. The primary labour statute, the Labour Act 2004, is human-centric and predates modern algorithmic management, recruitment screening tools, and "robo-firing". So in other words,  there is an absence of AI-Specific Employment Laws to tackle this growing aspect of our laws except for the Oversight statute which we rely upon,  the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023 and non-binding policy guides like the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS) of 2025.

Although direct AI rules are absent, employers and tech platforms can be challenged or scrutinized under broader legal frameworks such as    Sections 36, 37, and 42 of the 1999 Constitution which guarantees the right to a fair hearing, right to private life, and freedom from discrimination based on place of origin, sex, religion, ethnic group, or political opinion. Algorithmic bias that systematically disadvantages job applicants or workers based on these protected traits breaches constitutional principles. AI hiring or evaluation tool (e.g., resume-screening algorithms trained on biased historical data) systematically disadvantages protected groups, it can run afoul of constitutional equality principles, though direct enforcement against private algorithmic choices remains legally untested and ambiguous. 

As a support cast, the NDPA provides that a data subject shall not be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing (including profiling) that produces legal or similarly significant effects concerning them, unless there is human intervention and the logic of the decision can be contested.

Under Section 24–32 of the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023, a data subject has the right not to be subjected to decisions based solely on automated processing unless there is human intervention and the logic of the decision can be contested.

This mandates that employers using AI for performance tracking, promotions, or dismissals must maintain human oversight and allow workers an avenue to challenge automated verdicts.

However,  one of the core source of our employment laws which is the Labour Act, that governs general employment relations, contracts, and unfair termination is silent on algorithms, opaque algorithmic management (such as ride-hailing or gig-economy assignment algorithms) which now  leaves workers with limited statutory recourse under traditional unfair dismissal or due process doctrines. 

These lapses in our system creates Key risks of unregulated workplace AI in Nigeria.AI models trained on past male-dominated or ethnically skewed datasets can replicate and hide bias behind a veneer of "objectivity".

Every day, someone on LinkedIn reminds us: AI subtitles still cant match a professional human translator.

Yes. We know. 🙂

I spent 3 years translating and subtitling videos by hand. I know exactly what a great human subtitler brings to the table. Im not here to argue with that.

Im here to ask a different question: what does that last bit of quality actually cost you?

A professionally subtitled hour of video can take days and cost hundreds of dollars per language. Need it in 5 languages? Do the math. 😅

Now picture this instead:
→ Near-pro quality
→ 20 hours of video subtitled in a single day
→ In multiple languages
→ For a small fraction of the price

Personally? Id take that deal every single time. Spend a few minutes reviewing the key lines, fix the odd name or term, and hit publish.

And heres the part nobody talks about: for most creators, the real alternative to AI subtitles isnt a professional translator. Its no subtitles at all. Their video just stays in one language, forever.

To be clear, some fields cant compromise. Medical content. Legal contracts. Anything where one wrong word causes real damage. There, hire the pros. Always.

But a cooking channel? A marketing course? A podcast episode? Chasing 100% there is like hiring an architect to hang a shelf. 🔨
So where do you draw the line? When is almost perfect good enough for you?

Let's kick this series off with #Unfair Discrimination (MIT AI Risk 1.1)

An employer could be accountable for a rejection decision it never saw, made by a tool it did not build. 

MIT subdomain 1.1, unfair discrimination and misrepresentation, covers unequal treatment of individuals or groups by AI, often on the basis of race, gender or other characteristics. 

In Mobley v. Workday, a collective action in the Northern District of California, the applicant alleges he was rejected from more than 100 roles by employers using the vendors AI screening tools.

In 2024 the court allowed the claim to proceed on the theory that a vendor screening candidates on an employers behalf can be its agent. A nationwide age-discrimination collective was conditionally certified in May 2025, distribution of the class action notice to potential plaintiffs was authorised in February 2026, and the core discrimination claims are still live. Workday denies the allegations and says its tools do not make hiring decisions. Nothing is proven yet. 

For lawyers, risk and governance professionals, a few points stand out. 

Discrimination does not need a protected characteristic in the data.

A model trained on past hiring patterns can learn proxies: graduation year, employment gaps, keywords. At provider level, the vendor configures the ranking logic and holds most of the evidence about how it behaves. At deployer level, the feature may be switched on by default, with no one looking at rejection rates by age band. And the applicant can be rejected in minutes, without ever being told that AI was involved, which is what makes this risk so hard to detect from the inside. 

Practical steps:
➡️ Map where automated screening and ranking already sit in your hiring chain, including features enabled by default.
➡️ Test outcomes across protected groups before go-live and at intervals afterwards, not only the design intent of the tool.
➡️ Put bias-testing obligations, audit rights and evidence access into vendor contracts.
➡️ Keep human review meaningful and documented. For high-risk uses under the EU AI Act, this sits with the deployer, not the provider.
➡️ Consider in advance, how bias-testing work is commissioned and whether privilege applies. 

Buying the tool does not transfer the accountability.

How is your organisation testing what its hiring tools actually do, rather than what they are intended to do? 

Explore the risks: https://airisk.mit.edu/

#AIGovernance #ResponsibleAI #EmploymentLaw #AIRisk

One of the systems I recently built for Vino Design & Builds started with a pretty simple problem:

𝐁𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐨 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐥.
And every missed call is a potentially lost client.

So we built an 𝐀𝐈 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐭 that handles the first part of that conversation.

It answers common questions, checks the team's Google Calendar for availability, books meetings, and figures out 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬.

A call might be about a building contract, telemarketing, hiring, an existing project, or something else entirely.

Instead of just taking a message, the system classifies the call, syncs is to their CRM (GHL) and sends the owners a summary of the conversation so they know what happened and what needs to happen next.

The part I found most interesting was the result.

According to the owner, their onboarding rate has  𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 7% since putting it in place.

That's potentially tens of thousands of dollars in a single month they were losing out on just because they didn't have the time. 

Remember people, as much as we'd like, we cannot handle everything by ourselves.

SEVEN REASONS WHY HR DEPARTMENTS SHOULD TAKE AI SERIOUSLY ==============================================
For decades, HR was primarily about people, policies and paperwork. Today, HR is deeply dependent on technology. In fact, you could argue that AI has become part of HRs infrastructure. 

Here are seven reasons why every HR department should take AI seriously: 

1.  ▶️ YOUR CANDIDATES ARE ALREADY USING IT. Applicants polish CVs, draft cover letters, and rehearse interviews with AI. If HR doesnt understand these tools, it cant tell real skill from a well-prompted chatbot, or design hiring processes that still reveal who someone really is. 

2.  ▶️ AI CAN QUITELY INHERIT OLD BIASES. A screening tool trained on past hiring decisions may learn to prefer the same profiles the company always hired. HR is the conscience of fair hiring, so it needs to know enough to ask hard questions of any AI vendor before trusting the shortlist. 

3.  ▶️ EVERY JOB DESCRIPTION IS BEING REWRITTEN. Tasks that took hours now take minutes. HR will be asked which roles change, which skills matter next, and how to reskill people instead of replacing them. Thats a workforce redesign, and HR should be holding the pen. 

4.  ▶️ EMPLOYEES ARE USING AI WHETHER THERE'S A POLICY OR NOT. Staff are already pasting meeting notes, client data, and draft contracts into AI tools. Without clear guidelines from HR, quot;shadow AIquot; becomes a privacy risk and a confidentiality risk at the same time. 

5.  ▶️ FEAR OF AI IS NOW AN EMPOYEE WELLBEIGN ISSUE. Many people quietly worry their job is next. HR is best placed to replace rumour with honest communication, a reskilling path, and reassurance where its earned. Ignoring the anxiety doesnt make it go away; it just makes it spread. 

6.  ▶️ PERSONALISED GROWTH BECOMES POSSIBLE AT SCALE. AI can suggest learning paths, mentors, and internal roles tailored to each persons skills and ambitions. Instead of one training catalogue for everyone, every employee could have something close to a personal career coach. 

7.  ▶️ THE LAW IS CATCHING UP FAST. Regulations on AI in hiring and employee monitoring are emerging in many places, and the EUs AI Act treats recruitment tools as high-risk. HR will be accountable for how these tools are used on people, so it needs to understand them before a regulator asks.

A contract software developer should reduce handoffs, not add another one.
This week’s hiring posts include full-stack, mobile, AI, and remote contract roles. The titles vary, but the delivery problem is familiar: a team needs progress before it is ready for another permanent layer.

That is where the right contract developer can help.
In my work across Flutter, React, Node.js, and cloud, I’m most useful when I can take a product slice from an unclear requirement to a working release, while keeping the trade-offs visible to the team.

For a startup tech team, that might mean:

• shipping an MVP without overbuilding
• adding a mobile app to an existing SaaS product
• turning an AI application or LLM idea into a usable workflow
• strengthening a web application while the core team stays focused

The key is to hire for the delivery gap, not just the missing stack keyword. Scope, ownership, and the expected outcome should be clear before the first sprint.

AI just saved me $3k+.

That was the contract I was about to sign.

I was on a call with a guy I really liked.

And I was honestly ready to hire him.

He sounded exactly like the person I wanted for my outreach.

I'm testing a strategy that is not that popular, so I needed a specific type of person.

So I built an agent to help me find the best candidate.

It reads the conversation, but it does a lot more than that.

It researches the person and how they talk.

I gave it the call, and it came back with what I had missed.

- He failed the roleplay we did.
- He performed average on objection-handling.
- He responded vaguely when I asked him about past results.

I checked all of the AI reasoning, and it held up. 

Hiring him looked risky.

The agent gave me the logic. 

I made the call. 

I chose not to hire him.

Don’t get me wrong, AI still can't help in many situations.

But when you:

- choose the appropriate process, 
- give it the right guidance,
- give it enough context,

it can save you a ton of money, stress, and effort.

In my case, this would have cost me $3k+.

Plus wasted time, missed opportunities, and who knows how much lost business.

PS: How do you choose where to use AI?

Designers say they charge $100 to $149 an hour. The booking records say £385 a day, about $63 an hour.

Same profession. Same year. Two numbers that are off by a factor of two.

The first comes from the Fast Company and AIGA survey, 1,273 freelance designers, fieldwork February to April 2026. The second comes from YunoJuno's actual contract data, 182,000+ booking data points. One is what designers report. The other is what clients paid.

If you are staring at a blank line on a proposal, that gap is the whole problem.

Here's what nobody talks about with the survey number: it is self-selected. 57% of respondents had been designers for more than 15 years. 64% said they were not looking for a salaried job. People who feel good about their rates fill in rate surveys. People whose freelance business is dying do not.

Then Creative Boom polled 882 creative professionals and found nearly 47% of the self-employed ones earn under £30,000 a year. Fast Company says a third clear six figures. Both are true. They surveyed different crowds.

Three things eat the difference between your rate and your pay:

204 hours a year lost to admin (Smallpdf, 397 freelancers). 24% waiting two weeks or longer after invoicing. 15% reporting that 5% or more of what they invoice never arrives. A 5% write-off is a 5% pay cut before you have done anything wrong.

The number that actually surprised me was in YunoJuno's seniority spread. Midweight £343 a day. Director £448. Fifteen years of career progression buys you 31% more per day.

But colorists average £491 and artworkers £319. A 54% spread inside one discipline, in one year. Position beats tenure, and it is not close.

On AI: 62% of designers use it often or sometimes, nearly two thirds are worried about it, 70% think it is hurting quality. Among the 153 hiring managers, only 14% expect to need fewer freelancers next year. And the average design day rate went from £367 to £385, up 5%.

My read: AI has moved designer anxiety a long way and designer rates barely at all. That could change fast. It has not changed yet in any number I could verify.

I am in Augsburg billing US clients, so I get asked about the arbitrage constantly. It is a cushion, not a business model. It does not survive a 10% currency swing, and it dies the moment your pitch is "same work, cheaper."

The profession does not have a price. It has a wide flat spread with no centre. Anyone handing you one confident number is selling you a course.

Law firms have never measured what they produce. They measure how long it took. 

That worked for a century (okay, since the 1960s). The client paid for the time, legal was a credence good, and nobody had to agree on what the output was actually worth. Then firms started buying AI, at $100 to $300 per user per month before add-ons. 

Every one of those purchases comes down to a single question: was it worth what we paid? 

You need two numbers to answer that. What the work cost, and what it produced. 

Firms have the first: the timesheet (why its a terrible dataset is a post for another day). Some track realisation and write-offs too. But AI works at the task level, and the only thread from a task to the matter P&L is time. So for anything AI touches, the second number doesnt exist. 

For the last 2 years (3 if you were early) nobody minded. Licences came out of the innovation budget on conviction, and pilots were a dime a dozen. Now its renewal season. And the CFO is asking. 

3 months ago at iManage ConnectLive, Paul Twigg, Oliver Bethell, Rachel Coleman and I agreed on one thing: firms were measuring inputs. Token usage. Adoption. Not outcomes.

The vendors have noticed. Legora is hiring its first Value Engineer in London. Harvey has partnered with Lumio to model the AI-era law firm. 

Then theres pricing-shift. In June, Legora moved Agent Pro from seats to consumption. (Expect the rest to follow, whatever your contract says.) Sounds fairer, except consumption measures activity, not outcomes. 

An agent that loops through a data room four times bills more than one that gets it right first time. (a16zs OpenRouter data has agents burning nearly 5x the tokens humans do, up 14x since February. Not legal-specific, and mostly cheap cached tokens, but the meter is speeding up.) 

For sixty years, firms have billed clients for inputs on work the client couldnt easily judge. Consumption pricing flips the conversation; the firm is now the client. 

On hourly billing, an AI tool that works perfectly cuts revenue. The hours it saves are the junior hours on procedure work that roll up to partner profit. So was it worth it? depends on who keeps the saved time. For fixed fee: the firm. Hourly: the client. 

So why have firms not measured outcomes? Its hard (it is), but mostly the model and the incentives structure never asked them to. Maister called this the fat smoker problem. We know what to do. The payoff is far away. So we don't. 

Consumption pricing makes not knowing VERY expensive. Value has to be defined by type of work. Cost per contract reviewed? Measurable. A partners judgment on a bet-the-company dispute? No token meter/hourly billing will ever capture that. And if firms don't define their own unit of output, the vendors value model will be the only numbers in the room at renewal.

It's funny how I get turned down flatly by one agency for a role, but another agency thinks I'm a perfect fit for exactly the same contract based on the exact same CV.

IT hiring has been completely random for about 5 or 6 years now. It doesn't seem to matter how good a fit you are for a role, as the company can't write a job spec, the agency cannot understand the job spec (which is usually gibberish comprising dozens of unrelated skills), neither has any idea how to read a CV, and then the company has no idea how to interview, so it's moved from keyword matching to AI with a low-quality prompt, and above all you are treated as an inconvenience to be fleeced for a margin at every step of the torturous process.

That's basically where we are in IT now, while we chase technology, when we can't even deal with people.
